As the build cache grows without bound on the host disk, the in-memory metadata structures and index pointers often reside in a shared heap space where multiple threads access adjacent memory addresses. False sharing occurs when two or more CPU cores attempt to modify different variables that happen to reside on the same 64-byte cache line, forcing the hardware to perform expensive cache coherency traffic and invalidation cycles despite no logical data dependency existing between the threads. This prevents the hardware from triggering the MESI protocol's invalidation state when one thread updates a size counter while another thread reads an adjacent pointer. By ensuring that the memory alignment of these control structures matches or exceeds the CPU cache line size, the system avoids the performance cliff where increased cache size leads to increased interconnect contention. The batch job issues a query on one of those sockets and blocks. Because the client-side socket read timeout is longer than the job's per-chunk retry budget (or absent, relying on OS keepalive defaults of ~2 hours), the worker thread parks. The pool has, say, 20 connections, roughly a third of them pinned to node B; those threads park one by one as they are checked out. RESULT v1 | k7e1231a46d | Redis replication is asynchronous by default. A master acknowledges every write command the moment it executes locally, then propagates it to replicas in the background. If a replica lags, nothing in the normal protocol flags it: the master keeps answering PING with PONG, INFO shows the link up, and cluster tooling sees a healthy topology. When the master dies and the lagging replica is promoted, any writes that existed only on the old master's memory or its unsent replication backlog are gone. Clients that received OK acknowledgements for those writes have lost confirmed data — the cluster reports fine while it has already failed its durability job. The two states are distinguished by what has been acknowledged versus what has been replicated. "Healthy" means reachable and topologically consistent; "safe" means the promoted replica's replication offset actually covers every write the master acknowledged. These can diverge silently for seconds under load, network jitter, or a slow replica, and the divergence is invisible to liveness checks because liveness never inspects offsets. Misleading green signal: the master responding to PING/PONG and reporting a connected replica (or cluster state "ok" / replication link "up" in INFO replication). This only proves connectivity, not that the replica is current. Separating check: from a client, issue WAIT numreplicas timeout after a write, or compare the master's master_repl_offset against each replica's slave_repl_offset / master_repl_offset reported in INFO replication. If the replica's offset trails the master's acknowledged offset by more than your tolerance, or WAIT times out, the failover would lose acknowledged writes — that is the failing state, invisible to the green signal.
